channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: Using LLM as a Judge and LLM as a Jury to Advance Scalable, Clinically Validated Safety Evaluations of Model Responses to Users Demonstrating Psychosis, arXiv, 2026
item.description: Seven clinician informed safety criteria were developed and validated, then used to build a human consensus dataset of model responses to users showing signs of psychosis. Automated scoring by a single strong LLM judge tracked human consensus closely, with Cohen's kappa around .75, and slightly outperformed a majority vote jury of several models. The result gives mental health safety work a scalable, clinically grounded evaluation method rather than one off red teaming, and it treats psychosis as the primary case rather than an afterthought.

item.title: Identifying, Explaining, and Correcting Ableist Language with AI, CHI 2026
item.description: GPT-4o generations were compared against crowdsourced annotations from trained disability community members, then evaluated by disabled participants. Agreement was equal across human and AI annotations, but participants significantly preferred the AI for its narrative consistency and accessible style while still valuing the emotional depth and cultural grounding of human annotators. The authors release a nuanced ableism annotation dataset and argue for participatory, disability centered pipelines, noting one autistic participant's point that lived experience is not optional expertise.

item.title: Algorithmic Ableism and the Normative Body: Disability in the Age of Technocapitalist AI, Technology and Disability, 2026
item.description: A qualitative comparative analysis of Microsoft Seeing AI, Be My Eyes, Google Lookout, and Google Live Transcribe treats user manuals, help center documentation, interface structure, and promotional material as the evidence rather than model performance. Across all four, accessibility is framed as translating disabled bodies and senses into formats legible to dominant technological norms, privileging visual, auditory, and linguistic standardization while marginalizing multi channel communication, interdependence, and alternative sensory practice. The paper's methodological move is to name design discourse itself as a site of algorithmic ableism.

item.title: From Synthesis to Clinical Assistance: A Strategy Aware Agent Framework for Autism Intervention Based on Real Clinical Data, arXiv, 2026
item.description: The framework moves autism intervention agents past purely synthetic dialogue by grounding them in a real clinical dataset, with intervention strategy represented explicitly in the agent's planning rather than left implicit inside a prompt. Framing the target as clinical assistance rather than replacement matters in a subfield where tooling is often validated only on simulated interactions, and where the people being intervened on are rarely the ones evaluating whether the intervention was worth doing.

item.title: Beyond Ethics: How Inclusive Innovation Drives Economic Returns in Medical AI, arXiv, 2026
item.description: A multi institution perspective from authors at Toronto, Bordeaux, British Columbia, Caltech, MIT, King's College London, and RAND introduces the inclusive innovation dividend, the counterintuitive claim that designing medical AI for underrepresented populations returns strategic and economic value rather than only discharging a fairness obligation. That reframing matters for psychiatry and disability, where exclusion from training data is usually filed under ethics and therefore competes with commercial priorities instead of aligning with them.

item.title: When AI Becomes a Friend: Child Rights Risks, Harms, and Regulatory Responses to AI Chatbots and Companions, UNICEF, June 2026
item.description: Comparing Australia, Brazil, California, China, the European Union, and the United Kingdom as of May 2026, the brief finds convergence on risk assessment, age assurance, disclosure of non human status, restrictions on harmful content, and user reporting, and sharp divergence on whether access is restricted at the access layer or only at the output layer and whether enforcement is administrative, civil, or criminal. It flags that socially and emotionally vulnerable adolescents are the most likely to turn to companion systems, and calls for mandatory pre deployment testing and child rights impact assessments rather than reaction after harm.

item.title: The Dawn of AI in Mental Health: Balancing Innovation, Risk, and Regulation, Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking, 2026
item.description: Written out of the FDA Digital Health Advisory Committee meeting on generative AI in patient facing mental health tools, the piece notes that the agency has authorized no AI enabled medical device specifically for mental health despite more than 1,200 authorizations in radiology, cardiology, and elsewhere. It surveys the EU AI Act, UK MHRA guidance, WHO governance work, and Chinese and Australian rules, then argues for predetermined change control plans, adversarial pre market testing across diverse demographics, and adverse event reporting so adaptive models can improve without escaping review.

item.title: FDA Announces Sweeping Changes to Oversight of Wearables and AI Enabled Devices, STAT, January 2026
item.description: The agency will ease regulation of digital health products, softening its approach to clinical decision support software so that tools delivering a single recommendation can reach market without FDA review provided they meet the other exemption criteria. Commissioner Marty Makary framed the change around investor friendliness and moving at Silicon Valley speed, a posture that sits awkwardly beside the same agency's still unfinished framework for generative AI mental health devices.
